measurement_concept.probe_and_geometry: Immersion MIR-ATR fiber probe (e.g. diamond or ZrO2 ATR tip) inserted into the heated vessel so the crystal stays in contact with the resin; a separate temperature sensor at the same location.
measurement_concept.location: In the mixing vessel, at a representative position away from walls and stirrer.
measurement_concept.fiber_link: MIR light needs CIR or PIR fibers, not silica; the achievable MIR link length is an open question, since long cables are only stated for silica fibers.

risks.risk: Viscosity is not measured directly: the spectroscopic signal tracks cure chemistry, and the link between conversion and viscosity must be established and validated for this resin.
The dark, strongly absorbing matrix may give weak or background-dominated Raman or fluorescence signals, so M2 may fail on the real resin.
ATR samples only a surface layer a few micrometres deep, so curing resin building up on the crystal and surface representativeness are real fouling and bias risks.
Any calibration is specific to this resin matrix and must be re-validated if the formulation changes.

steps.step: Measure each sample with the MIR-ATR fiber probe and, in parallel, with the Raman probe; record temperature with an independent sensor.
steps.purpose: Test the single methods first on identical material.

steps.step: Measure viscosity of each sample with an independent laboratory rheometer as the reference method.
steps.purpose: Provide the reference against which any spectroscopic viscosity inference is judged.

steps.step: Build a calibration from cure spectra to the rheometer reference, validate on held-out batches, and only then test the MIR+Raman fusion against the best single method.
steps.purpose: Confirm that combining methods actually adds accuracy before adding hardware.

steps.step: Agree go/no-go criteria with the customer: the required end-point accuracy and response time from Q1 decide whether the spectroscopic inference is acceptable or an independent viscometer is needed.

solution_options.fusion_note: Low-level fusion: MIR-ATR and Raman spectra from the same probe spot merged into one matrix after synchronisation to a common time step and block scaling. Each method keeps its own calibration and diagnostics. The fused model must beat the best single method on held-out batches, otherwise the extra instrument is dropped.

chemometrics_note: A PLS-type calibration from MIR (and optionally Raman) spectra to the rheometer viscosity reference is needed, built on representative curing batches and validated on held-out runs; the calibration is matrix-specific.
realtime_tracking_note: Continuous in-line tracking of the cure signal plus temperature is the goal; the stop decision should use the validated model output with the customer's end-point criterion.
future_direction: If the correlation proves robust, a simplified LED- or filter-based spectral sensor at the vessel could replace the full spectrometer later.

proposal.what_would_change_it: If the customer's end-point accuracy (Q1) is tight, an independent in-line viscometer becomes necessary alongside spectroscopy; if the resin fluoresces strongly, Raman may drop out and the choice narrows to MIR-ATR alone.
proposal.next_step: Run the feasibility trial: MIR-ATR and Raman spectra plus temperature on representative curing samples with rheometer reference, then agree go/no-go criteria.

brief_answer: Test an immersion MIR-ATR fiber probe first: it suits dark, thick pastes and tracks the cure chemistry from which viscosity must be inferred, with a separate temperature sensor. Test a Raman probe on the same batches as a comparison. Spectroscopy cannot measure viscosity directly, so a rheometer reference is needed to calibrate the end point. Open: your target viscosity and accuracy, vessel access and temperature range, and whether the resin fluoresces.
